'''Charles Bradley Moore''' (born December 7, 1939) is an American chemist and research administrator. His research focused on the application of lasers to understand the behavior and reaction dynamics of energized molecules and energy transfer between molecules. He is currently professor emeritus of chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he had a long career as a faculty member actively engaged in research (1963–2000).<ref name=quant>{{cite journal|journal=Journal of Physical Chemistry A|volume=104|page=45|title=Biography of Professor C. Bradley Moore|year=2000|issue=45 |doi=10.1021/jp002080z|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/jp002080z|url-access=subscription}}</ref> While at UC Berkeley, Moore also served in several administrative roles, including chair of the department of chemistry (1982–1986), dean of the college of chemistry (1988–1994), and director of the chemical sciences division at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] (1998–2000).<ref name=quant/> He was vice president for research at [[Ohio State University]] (2000–2003) and held the same position at [[Northwestern University]] (2004–2008).<ref>{{cite news |title=C. Bradley Moore |url=https://www.osa.org/en-us/history/biographies/bios/c_bradley_moore/ |access-date=November 3, 2020 |publisher=Optical Society of America}}</ref> He is also professor emeritus at Northwestern. Moore is a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].

==Early life and education==
Brad Moore was born in [[Boston]] on December 7, 1939, and raised in [[Pennsylvania]]. He attended [[Phillips Exeter Academy]] in New Hampshire for high school, and earned his AB at [[Harvard]] in 1960. He did his PhD thesis research at UC Berkeley under the supervision of [[George C. Pimentel]], and joined the Berkeley faculty immediately after defending his thesis in 1963.<ref name=quant/>

==Notable accomplishments==
In the 1960s, Moore was one of the first chemists to utilize the newly invented [[laser]] in chemical research, later editing the five-volume series "Chemical and Biochemical Applications of Lasers".<ref>{{cite book | isbn=978-0125054058 | title=Chemical and Biochemical Applications of Lasers | last1=Moore | first1=Charles Bradley | year=1974 }}</ref> His group developed a method for isotopic enrichment using laser excitation.<ref>{{cite journal|author=C.B. Moore|title=Applications of lasers to isotope separation|journal=Acc. Chem. Res.|year=1973|volume=6, 9|issue=9|pages=323–328|doi=10.1021/ar50069a007|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ar50069a007|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In the 1980s, his research group was the first to measure quantum state-resolved unimolecular reaction rates, and to see indications that reaction rates are quantized as suggested by [[RRKM theory]]. Attempts to explain his experimental observations motivated theoretical/computational advances, e.g. by his colleague [[William Hughes Miller]] and by Stephen Klippenstein. Moore also proposed the roaming radical mechanism<ref>AG Suits, Acc Chem Res. 2008 Jul;41(7):873-81. doi: 10.1021/ar8000734.</ref> to explain unexpected product formation in unimolecular decomposition reactions, and his experiments demonstrated that nuclear spin is conserved through chemical reactions.

Moore's research was well-respected by the physical chemistry community. Two chapters of the ''Annual Review of Physical Chemistry'' are devoted to reviewing his research.<ref>{{cite journal|author=C.B. Moore|journal=Annu. Rev. Phys. Chem.|title=A Spectroscopist's View of Energy States, Energy Transfers, and Chemical Reactions|year=2007|volume=58|pages=1–33|doi=10.1146/annurev.physchem.58.032806.104610|pmid=17034339|bibcode=2007ARPC...58....1M|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>W.H. Green, C.B. Moore, W.F. Polik, Ann. Rev. Phys. Chem 1992</ref> The ''Journal of Physical Chemistry A'''s Nov. 16, 2000 issue was a festschrift published in his honor,<ref name=quant/> and the [[American Chemical Society]] held a special symposium in his honor at its National Meeting in August 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/meetings.html|title=ACS Meetings & Events|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=November 3, 2020}}</ref> He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1986,<ref>{{cite news |title=C. Bradley Moore |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/c-bradley-moore-ppce16/ |access-date=November 3, 2020 |publisher=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref> and to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1996.<ref>{{cite news |title=Professor C. Bradley Moore |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/c-bradley-moore |access-date=November 3, 2020 |publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Brad Moore has been married to Penny Percival Moore, an educator, since 1960. They raised two children, now adults. Brad's father, Charles Walden Moore, worked for a time as a laboratory assistant to [[Thomas Edison]].<ref name=quant/>
